tagline: South through Maryland on an assassin's trail to the Potomac.
intro: The route leaves Washington the way John Wilkes Booth did on the night of April 14, 1865, after he shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre and broke his leg leaping to the stage. He crossed the Navy Yard Bridge on horseback, met David Herold, and the two fled south toward the Potomac, eluding Federal troops for nearly two weeks. The byway follows them by Clinton, Waldorf and Bryantown.
The road also passes Underground Railroad sites in Southern Maryland. The jail at Port Tobacco held so many freedom seekers that it earned the name Reverse Underground Railroad.

moments.title: Surratt House, Clinton
moments.text: Carbines from an earlier plot to kidnap Lincoln were hidden at this tavern, where Booth and Herold stopped for supplies, and Mary Surratt was hanged in 1865 for her part.

moments.title: Dr. Samuel A. Mudd House
moments.text: The country doctor set Booth's broken leg here on April 15 and let him stay the night, and it sent Mudd to prison in the Dry Tortugas.

moments.title: Popes Creek
moments.text: From this shore the two set out across the Potomac, rowed by mistake into Nanjemoy Creek, spent the night there and crossed to Virginia later.
